**Data Analytics for AI · Executive M.Tech · IIT Jammu**  
**Module 01 · Fundamentals of Probability and Random Signal Theory**

[Main lecture notes](02-random-variables.qmd) · [Probability-space supplement](01-probability-supplement.qmd) · [01.3 tutorial: coins, records and ticket durations](02-joint-distributions-tutorial.qmd) · [01.4 meeting problem](04-meeting-problem.qmd)

This supplement gives proofs and qualifications for the calculations in Lecture 01.2. The main notes contain the definitions needed for routine problem solving. All application models remain stipulated teaching models. Independent exercises appear without solutions.

## 1. Laws, PMFs and densities

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ a measurable function. Its law is

$$P_X(B)=P(X\in B),\qquad B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R).$$

If a countable set $S$ satisfies $P(X\in S)=1$, the law is discrete. Countable additivity applied to disjoint events $\{X=x\}$ gives

$$P_X(B)=\sum_{x\in S\cap B}p_X(x),\qquad p_X(x)=P(X=x).$$

In particular, $\sum_{x\in S}p_X(x)=1$. The PMF can be set to zero off $S$. $X$ may take values outside $S$ on a $P$-null set of outcomes; the countable support describes where the law places mass.

A law is **absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure** if it admits a measurable nonnegative density $f_X$ satisfying

$$P_X(B)=\int_B f_X(x)\,dx\quad\text{for every Borel }B.$$

It follows that $\int_{\mathbb R}f_X=1$. Densities differing only on a set of Lebesgue measure zero describe the same law. Their values at individual endpoints have no effect on probabilities.

### Why “no point masses” is not the full density condition

Every law with a density has $P(X=x)=0$ for each $x$. The converse does not hold in full generality: there are singular continuous laws with no atoms and no density with respect to length. The main lecture deliberately confines its continuous calculations to laws admitting PDFs.

A useful boundary case is a **mixed law**. An irrigation planner needs to distinguish a completely dry day from a day with some rain. Let $R$ be the daily rainfall in millimetres at a fixed field location. A zero reading represents no rain; positive amounts vary continuously in this simplified model. For a day selected under the stipulated rainfall model, let $P(R=0)=0.3$ and, given a positive amount, let $R$ be uniform on $(0,10)$ mm. Then for Borel $B$,

$$P(R\in B)=0.3\,\mathbf1_{\{0\in B\}}
+0.07\int_{B\cap(0,10)}dr.$$

The continuous component integrates to $0.7$; the remaining $0.3$ is an atom at zero. This law cannot be represented by an ordinary PDF alone. Its CDF is

$$F_R(r)=\begin{cases}
0,&r<0,\\
0.3+0.07r,&0\le r<10,\\
1,&r\ge10.
\end{cases}$$

In particular $P(R>5)=0.35$. A function that merely equals $0.07$ on $(0,10)$ misses the dry-day mass.

## 2. CDF properties and endpoints

For any real-valued random variable, $F_X(x)=P(X\le x)$. If $a<b$, the disjoint decomposition

$$\{X\le b\}=\{X\le a\}\cup\{a<X\le b\}$$

gives $P(a<X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a)$. Define

$$F_X(a^-)=\lim_{t\uparrow a}F_X(t)=P(X<a).$$

Then

$$P(a\le X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a^-),\qquad
P(X=a)=F_X(a)-F_X(a^-).$$

The continuity properties follow from continuity of probability on monotone sequences of events. For example, $\{X\le x+1/n\}$ decreases to $\{X\le x\}$, so $F_X(x+1/n)\to F_X(x)$, establishing right continuity. The events $\{X\le n\}$ increase to $\Omega$, while $\{X\le-n\}$ decrease to the empty set; hence the limiting values are 1 and 0.

If a PDF exists, $F_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x f_X(t)dt$ is absolutely continuous and $F_X'=f_X$ almost everywhere. An arbitrary CDF need not have this property. In particular, differentiating the rainfall CDF away from zero cannot recover its atom.

## 3. Marginalization and normalization

Let $X,Y$ be discrete on countable sets $S_X,S_Y$. For fixed $x$, the events $\{X=x,Y=y\}$, as $y$ varies, are disjoint and their union agrees with $\{X=x\}$ up to a null event. Thus

$$p_X(x)=\sum_{y\in S_Y}p_{X,Y}(x,y).$$

Summing in $x$ gives $\sum_xp_X(x)=1$. Nonnegative series may be summed in either order. The corresponding proof applies to $p_Y$.

For a jointly absolutely continuous pair with density $f_{X,Y}$, define

$$g(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy.$$

Tonelli's theorem permits the iterated integral because the integrand is measurable and nonnegative. For Borel $B$,

$$P(X\in B)=\iint_{B\times\mathbb R}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy
=\int_B g(x)\,dx.$$

Therefore $g$ is a version of the marginal density $f_X$, and $\int g=1$. A density may be infinite on a null set, but is finite almost everywhere when its integral is 1. These exceptional values can be redefined without changing the law.

The support bounds must be retained. For the main lecture's maintenance model, integrating over $0<y<x<1$ gives $f_X(x)=2x$ on $(0,1)$ and $f_Y(y)=2(1-y)$ on $(0,1)$, both zero elsewhere. Extending the density value 2 across the whole unit square would double its total mass.

## 4. Conditional distributions and their scope

### Discrete conditioning

For $p_X(x)>0$,

$$p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_X(x)}.$$

Nonnegativity is inherited from the joint PMF, and

$$\sum_y p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)
=\frac{\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_X(x)}=1.$$

Multiplying by $p_X(x)$ and summing over positive-mass $x$ gives the law of total probability:

$$p_Y(y)=\sum_{x:p_X(x)>0}p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)p_X(x).$$

When $p_X(x)=0$, the ratio is undefined. Assignments of a conditional distribution at those values do not affect the joint law or any of the resulting unconditional probabilities.

### Conditioning with a joint density

For $0<f_X(x)<\infty$, set

$$f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)}.$$

For almost every such $x$, this is a probability density in $y$. It reconstructs joint probabilities through

$$P(X\in B,Y\in C)
=\int_B\left(\int_C f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)\,dy\right)f_X(x)\,dx.$$

This identity is a precise way to characterize a conditional-density version. Values on an $X$-null set can be changed without changing the identity. Consequently the law alone does not uniquely prescribe conditional distributions at every individual continuous conditioning value. Smooth textbook formulas choose a natural version.

For a fixed Borel set $C$, let $g_C(u)=\int_C f_{X,Y}(u,y)dy$. If $g_C$ and $f_X$ are continuous at $x$ and $f_X(x)>0$, then

$$\begin{aligned}
P(Y\in C\mid x-\epsilon<X<x+\epsilon)
&=\frac{\int_{x-\epsilon}^{x+\epsilon}g_C(u)du}
{\int_{x-\epsilon}^{x+\epsilon}f_X(u)du}\\
&\longrightarrow\frac{g_C(x)}{f_X(x)}
=\int_C f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)dy.
\end{aligned}$$

Divide numerator and denominator by $2\epsilon$ and use continuity to justify the limit. This supports the narrow-band interpretation used for the maintenance model at interior durations. It does not divide an event probability by $P(X=x)$.

For a band $B$ with $P(X\in B)>0$, an unambiguous conditional density of $Y$ is

$$f_{Y\mid X\in B}(y)=
\frac{\int_B f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx}{P(X\in B)}.$$

This averages over the selected durations with their appropriate weights; it is generally not the conditional density at the band's midpoint. In the uniform triangular model, the probability of $Y<c$ given $a<X<b$ does coincide with the midpoint-conditioned probability when $0<c\le a<b<1$. That coincidence for these thresholds does not make the two conditional distributions identical.

## 5. Independence and factorization

Random variables $X,Y$ are independent if

$$P(X\in B,Y\in C)=P(X\in B)P(Y\in C)$$

for every pair of Borel sets $B,C$. In the discrete case, applying this to singleton sets gives the PMF factorization. Conversely, summing a factorized PMF over $B\times C$ proves the definition.

For a pair with a joint density, independence is equivalent to $f_{X,Y}=f_Xf_Y$ almost everywhere. For the sufficient direction, integrate the product over $B\times C$ and separate the integrals. For the necessary direction, independence makes the joint law the product of the marginal laws, which has density $f_Xf_Y$; uniqueness of a density up to null sets gives the result.

A single unequal cell proves dependence in a discrete table. For densities, a discrepancy at one isolated point proves nothing because density values can be changed on null sets. In the maintenance example the discrepancy occupies a rectangle of positive area, so the argument in the main notes establishes dependence.

### Continuous marginals need not imply a joint PDF

Suppose a data logger stores a normalized sensor reading $U$ and a second field $V$ that is an exact copy of the same reading. This is one measurement stored twice, not two separate sensor measurements. Stipulate that $U$ is uniform on $(0,1)$ and put $V=U$. Both marginals have uniform densities, but the pair lies on the diagonal $v=u$ with probability 1. That diagonal has plane area zero, so no ordinary two-dimensional PDF can represent this joint law. The main lecture's joint-PDF formulas assume that a joint density exists, not merely that each marginal has one.

## Gap transformations for the meeting problem {#meeting-time-transformation}

The [01.4 worked example](04-meeting-problem.qmd) uses the gap $D=|T_A-T_B|$. Suppose $T_A,T_B$ are independent, identically distributed on $[0,1]$, with density $h$, extended by zero outside that interval. Their joint density is $h(a)h(b)$.

For $Z=T_B-T_A$, use the transformation $(a,b)\mapsto(a,z)$ with $b=a+z$ and absolute Jacobian determinant 1. Integrating out $a$ gives a density version

$$f_Z(z)=\int_{\mathbb R}h(a)h(a+z)\,da.$$

Identical marginals and independence make this density symmetric. For $0<d<1$, folding the positive and negative gaps gives

$$f_D(d)=f_Z(d)+f_Z(-d)=2\int_0^{1-d}h(a)h(a+d)\,da.$$

The original joint law assigns zero mass to the diagonal, so $P(D=0)=0$; there is no omitted atom when folding. The density is zero off $[0,1]$, and choices at endpoints are immaterial. With independent but different marginal densities, retain both integrals instead of doubling one. With dependence, use the actual joint density if one exists; the product formula is not justified.

For uniform marginals $h(a)=1$ on $[0,1]$, the integral is $2(1-d)$, matching the CDF derivation in the worked example.

For $h(a)=2(1-a)$ on $[0,1]$, put $u=1-d-a$:

$$\begin{aligned}
f_{D,E}(d)
&=8\int_0^{1-d}(1-a)(1-a-d)\,da\\
&=8\int_0^{1-d}(d+u)u\,du\\
&=4d(1-d)^2+\frac83(1-d)^3
=\frac83-4d+\frac43d^3.
\end{aligned}$$

The factored expression shows nonnegativity on $(0,1)$. Its integral is

$$\left[\frac83d-2d^2+\frac13d^4\right]_0^1=1.$$

Thus, on $0\le d\le1$,

$$F_{D,E}(d)=\frac83d-2d^2+\frac13d^4
=1-(1-d)^3\left(1+\frac d3\right),$$

with CDF 0 below 0 and 1 above 1. This is the formula used by the interactive waiting-time demonstration. It is continuous at both endpoints, gives $139/256$ at $d=1/4$, and does not confuse the arrival density with the gap density.

## 6. Advanced exercises

**S1. Mixed rainfall model.** For the model in Section 1, calculate $P(R=0)$, $P(0<R\le2)$, $P(R\le2)$ and $P(R>5\mid R>0)$. Explain why differentiating the CDF away from zero loses information.

**S2. A narrow-band limit.** In the maintenance triangle, take $0<\epsilon<1/4$. Calculate $P(X>3/4\mid1/2-\epsilon<Y<1/2+\epsilon)$ by integrating over regions. Take the limit as $\epsilon\downarrow0$, derive the natural conditional density of $X$ given $Y=1/2$, and verify agreement.

**S3. Null-set changes.** In the uniform sensor-square model, change the joint density value at $(0,0)$ from $1/4$ to 100. Does the probability law change? Does independence change? Explain using integration.

**S4. Continuous marginals without a joint density.** For $V=U$ with $U$ uniform on $(0,1)$, calculate $P(U\le1/2,V\le1/2)$ and compare it with the product of the marginals. Explain both dependence and the absence of a two-dimensional PDF.
